zone: Buckhorn, Marmot Pass and the Dungeness crest — eastern Olympics
_areas_note: All five peaks stay in the zone, but the trailhead attribution in the brief needed correcting. Buckhorn Mountain is served by the Upper Big Quilcene trailhead over Marmot Pass; Mount Worthington by the Tubal Cain trailhead and Buckhorn Lake; Mount Townsend by its own trailhead on the Quilcene side. Warrior Peak and Inner Constance are indeed Home Lake objectives rather than Lake Constance ones, but the practical trailhead for Home Lake is the UPPER DUNGENESS, not the Dosewallips — the Dungeness approach is walked in one long day on maintained trail while the Dosewallips still carries the washed-out road walk, so almost nobody comes at Home Lake from the south. Boulder Shelter on the Dungeness side is also reachable in 1.7 miles over Marmot Pass, which is what ties this whole zone to one crest. Inner Constance is the one peak that genuinely lives in two zones: its northwest side is a Home Lake climb and belongs here, while the northeast summit reached over Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a Lake Constance climb and belongs to the Constance file. I have deliberately NOT repeated Lake Constance or the Dosewallips road-end staging camps, both of which that file already covers properly. Home Lake IS repeated, because the earlier file describes it only as a bail-out for Mount Constance and explicitly says it is the wrong basin there — for these two peaks it is the primary high camp, and it is reached from a different trailhead entirely. No peak was excluded.

sites.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
sites.capacity: A scatter of established sites among the firs, perhaps eight to ten tents spread out along the trail; busy but rarely truly full
sites.water: The reason to stop here. A stream runs through camp and is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the whole approach — everything above is dry ground. Fill for the summit day here, not at the pass.
sites.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. No advance permit and no fee to camp — sign the free self-issued register at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Group limit is twelve. OPEN FIRES ARE PROHIBITED above 3,500 ft, which includes this camp, so bring a stove and do not gather wood.
sites.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. Camping here rather than at the pass costs you the sunset and the view and buys you water, tree cover and shelter from wind, which on this crest is not a small trade. Below it, Shelter Rock Camp at 2.6 miles and about 3,600 ft is the wet-weather fallback if you start late. The season is roughly late June through October; snow lingers in the upper basin into early summer and the trail above camp is exposed once it leaves the trees.

sites.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
sites.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded
sites.water: NONE. This is a dry camp and it is the single most common mistake made here — late-season accounts describe not a puddle or a patch of snow anywhere near the pass. Carry everything up from Camp Mystery, which is the last source half a mile below.
sites.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires at this elevation. No quota and no reservation.
sites.notes: The obvious camp for anyone whose objective is Buckhorn Mountain and who is willing to haul water, because the summit path leaves directly from the pass and a party sleeping here is on top for sunrise with an hour of walking. It is also the hinge of this whole zone: the trail carries on over the pass and drops 1.7 miles down to Boulder Shelter, which is how a Quilcene-side party reaches the Warrior and Inner Constance country without driving around to the Dungeness. The cost of camping this high is real — the pass is a wind funnel with no tree cover, weather arrives with no warning off the Dungeness side, and the meadows here are fragile enough that you should use an existing pad rather than making a new one. Snow-free from roughly early July; a spring ascent on skis or snowshoes is common but then the pass is a genuine winter camp.

sites.name: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington
sites.capacity: Modest, three or four small sites in dark timber at the lake; the Tubal Cain mine area lower down holds more parties if this is taken
sites.water: Reliable at the lake all season. It is a shallow forested tarn rather than running water, so filter it, and there is nothing above once you start up toward the saddle.
sites.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park at the Tubal Cain trailhead. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft. No quota, no reservation, no bear canister requirement on this side of the divide — though the mine area sees enough traffic that hanging or canistering food is sensible anyway.
sites.notes: Mount Worthington has no maintained trail to its summit and no route that anyone would call standard, so the camp does most of the work. Buckhorn Lake sits about half a mile off the Tubal Cain trail on a spur leaving at roughly five and a half to six miles, and from it the usual line crosses the outlet, works around the south end of the lake on a discontinuous path through moderate brush, climbs south into an open basin near 5,260 ft, and then heads up to the saddle between Worthington and Iron Mountain — the 6,938 ft summit is off-trail scrambling and routefinding from there. Camping lower at the old mine workings adds several hundred feet and a couple of miles to the morning; camping higher is not really an option, since above the lake there is neither water nor level ground until the ridge. Scope the descent line on the walk in, because it is much harder to identify from above. Best from July into October once the brush is dry and the basin has melted out.

sites.name: Camp Windy, below Mount Townsend
sites.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families
sites.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
sites.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
sites.notes: The only real camp on Mount Townsend, sitting somewhere around 5,200 ft at roughly two and a half to three miles up the trail — published elevations for it vary by about a hundred feet, which is fair given it is a spread of sites rather than a point. Townsend is a walk-up by its standard trail and most parties do it as a day hike, so the case for camping is weather, an early start for the view east over Puget Sound, or linking it with the Silver Lakes basin. The switchbacks above camp reach the Silver Lakes junction near 5,500 ft at about three miles, and those lakes at roughly 5,400 ft are the quieter alternative if Camp Windy is full — but they sit in a side valley and add distance to the summit rather than saving any. Above camp the trail breaks out onto open, wind-scoured slopes to the 6,280 ft south summit; the name of the camp is not decorative, and a tent pitched carelessly here will not survive the night.

sites.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
sites.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards
sites.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
sites.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
sites.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.

sites.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
sites.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits
sites.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
sites.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
sites.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
